text: My father founded the company in 1978.
We have completed forty buildings since then.
He took over the direction three years ago.
The firm has never had an outside partner.
The firm has never taken outside capital.
We diversified into renovation work in 2016.
My uncle and I hold equal stakes, so neither of us decides alone.

My grandmother founded this company in 1961, in a building we still use, and I will tell you what has not changed since: the building, and the recipe. Everything else has. I am the third generation, which sounds impressive until you find out how few of us there are. The year I would rather not talk about is 2014. My father got sick very suddenly and there was no succession plan, not one page, and for a while three different people in the family believed they were in charge. Nobody was lying. Nobody had ever written it down. That year cost us eighteen months and the biggest client we had. So what I have done since is unglamorous. I have written everything down, and I have brought in two people from outside the family, which my grandmother would have found insulting and which has saved us twice. My advice, if you want it, is to have the conversation while it is still boring. It is never boring later.

I go into a lot of family companies, and I ask the same question in the first meeting: who decides? It sounds rude. It is the most useful ninety seconds of the year. If two people answer at the same time and give different names, I already know where that year is going to go. The blind spot is almost always the same one. Owners confuse ownership with authority, and those are not the same thing at all. It is not that they disagree about the decision. It is that nobody has ever written down who gets to make it, and an argument about who decides costs more than any bad decision I have ever seen taken. On hiring, the companies that have survived into a third generation almost all brought somebody in from outside early, before they needed to. And afterwards they say the same thing. They do not regret hiring that person. They regret the years they spent deciding to.
My father founded the company in 1978.
We have completed forty buildings since then.
The company has weathered three downturns.
We diversified into renovation work in 2016.
The firm has never taken outside capital.
Have you ever brought somebody in from outside the family?
My uncle and I hold equal stakes, so neither of us decides alone.
